title: VI. The First Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: This was the third time Ivan had been to see Smerdyakov since his return from Moscow. The first time he had seen him and talked with him was the day he arrived; he had visited him once more a fortnight later. But his visits had ended with that second one, so that it was now over a month since he had seen him. And he had heard scarcely anything about him.

Ivan had only returned five days after his father's death, so he was not present at the funeral, which had taken place the day before he came back. The cause of his delay was that Alyosha, not knowing his Moscow address, had had to apply to Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph to him, and she, not knowing his address either, telegraphed her sister and aunt, reckoning that Ivan would go to see them as soon as he reached Moscow. But he didn't go to them until four days after his arrival. When he got the telegram, he had, of course, set off post-haste to our town. The first to meet him was Alyosha, and Ivan was greatly surprised to find that, contrary to the general opinion of the town, Alyosha refused to entertain any suspicion against Mitya and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later on, after seeing the police captain and the prosecutor, and hearing the details of the charge and the arrest, he was still more surprised at Alyosha, and put his opinion down to exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, of whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond.

By the way, let us say a word or two about Ivan's feelings toward his brother Dmitri. He positively disliked him; at most, he sometimes felt a compassion for him, and even that was mixed with great contempt, almost revulsion. Mitya's whole personality, even his appearance, was extremely unattractive to him. Ivan looked with indignation on Katerina Ivanovna's love for his brother. Yet he went to see Mitya on his first day back, and that interview, far from shaking his belief in Mitya's guilt, positively strengthened it. He found his brother agitated, nervously excited. Mitya had been talkative, but very distracted and incoherent. He used violent language, accused Smerdyakov, and was fearfully muddled. He talked mostly about the three thousand roubles which he said had been “stolen” from him by his father.
“The money was mine, it was my money,” Mitya kept repeating. “Even if I had stolen it, I would have had the right.”

He hardly contested the evidence against him, and when he did try to turn a fact to his advantage, it was in an absurd and incoherent way. He hardly seemed to wish to defend himself to Ivan or anyone else. Quite the contrary — he was angry and proudly scornful of the charges against him; he kept firing up and abusing everyone. He only laughed contemptuously at Grigory's evidence about the open door, and declared that it was “the devil that opened it.” But he couldn't bring forward any coherent explanation of the fact. He even succeeded in insulting Ivan during their first meeting, telling him sharply that it was not for people who declared that “everything was lawful” to suspect and question him. Altogether he was anything but friendly with Ivan on that occasion. Immediately after that interview with Mitya, Ivan went for the first time to see Smerdyakov.

On the train coming from Moscow, he had kept thinking of Smerdyakov and of his last conversation with him the evening before he'd gone away. Many things seemed puzzling and suspicious to him. But when he gave his evidence to the investigating lawyer, Ivan said nothing for the time being about that conversation. He put that off until he had seen Smerdyakov, who was at the time in the hospital.

Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, confidently asserted in reply to Ivan's persistent questions that Smerdyakov's epileptic attack was unmistakably genuine, and they were surprised that Ivan should ask whether he might have been shamming on the day of the catastrophe. They gave him to understand that the attack had been an exceptional one, the fits persisting and recurring several times, so that the patient's life had positively been in danger, and only now, after remedies had been applied, could they state with confidence that the patient would survive. “Though it might well be,” Doctor Herzenstube added, “that his reason will be impaired for a considerable period, if not permanently.” On Ivan's asking impatiently whether that meant Smerdyakov was now mad, they told him that this wasn't yet the case in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities could be observed. Ivan decided to find out for himself what those abnormalities were.

At the hospital he was immediately allowed to see the patient. Smerdyakov was lying on a truckle bed in a separate ward. There was only one other bed in the room, and in it lay a tradesman of the town, swollen with dropsy, who was obviously near death; he could be no hindrance to their conversation. Smerdyakov grinned uncertainly on seeing Ivan, and for the first instant seemed nervous. So at least Ivan fancied. But that was only momentary. For the rest of the time Ivan was struck, on the contrary, by Smerdyakov's composure. From the first glance Ivan had no doubt that he was very ill. He was very weak; he spoke slowly, seeming to move his tongue with difficulty; he was much thinner and sallower. Throughout the interview, which lasted twenty minutes, he kept complaining of headache and of pain in all his limbs. His thin emasculate face seemed to have grown so tiny; his hair was ruffled, and his crest of curls in front stood up in a thin tuft. But in the left eye, which was screwed up and seemed to be insinuating something, Smerdyakov showed himself unchanged. “It's always worth while speaking to a clever man.” Ivan was reminded of that at once. He sat down on the stool at his feet. Smerdyakov, with painful effort, shifted his position in bed, but he was not the first to speak. He remained mute, and didn't even look much interested.
“Can you talk to me?” Ivan asked. “I won't tire you much.”
“Certainly I can,” Smerdyakov mumbled, in a faint voice. “Has your honor been back long?” he added patronizingly, as though encouraging a nervous visitor.
“I only arrived today. To see the mess you're all in here.”
Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why do you sigh? You knew about it all along,” Ivan blurted out.
Smerdyakov was stolidly silent for a while.
“How could I help knowing? It was clear beforehand. But how could I tell it would turn out like that?”
“What would turn out? Don't prevaricate! You foretold you'd have a fit — on the way down to the cellar, you remember. You mentioned the very spot.”
“Have you said so at the examination yet?” Smerdyakov asked with composure.
Ivan suddenly felt angry.
“No, I haven't yet — but I certainly shall. You must explain a great deal to me, my man; and let me tell you, I'm not going to let you play with me!”
“Why should I play with you, when I put my whole trust in you, as in God Almighty?” said Smerdyakov, with the same composure, only closing his eyes for a moment.

“In the first place,” Ivan began, “I know that epileptic fits can't be predicted beforehand. I've inquired; don't try to take me in. You can't foretell the day and the hour. How is it you told me the day and the hour beforehand, and about the cellar, too? How could you tell you would fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, if you didn't sham a fit on purpose?”

“I had to go to the cellar anyway — several times a day, in fact,” Smerdyakov drawled deliberately. “I fell from the garret in just the same way a year ago. It's quite true you can't predict the day and hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a presentiment of it.”
“But you did foretell the day and the hour!”
“As to my epilepsy, sir, you had much better ask the doctors here. You can ask them whether it was a real fit or a sham; it's no use my saying any more about it.”
“And the cellar? How could you know beforehand about the cellar?”

“You don't seem able to let go of that cellar! As I was going down to the cellar, I was in terrible dread and doubt. What frightened me most was losing you and being left without defense in the whole world. So I went down into the cellar thinking, ‘Here, it'll come on any moment, it'll strike me down any moment — will I fall?' And it was through this fear that I suddenly felt the spasm that always comes ... and so I went flying. All of that, and all of our previous conversation at the gate the evening before, when I told you how frightened I was and spoke of the cellar — I told all of it to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it's all been written down in the protocol. And the doctor here, Mr. Varvinsky, insisted to all of them that it was the very thought of it that brought it on, the apprehension that I might fall. It was just then that the fit seized me. And so they've written it down, that this is how it must have happened, simply out of my fear.”
As he finished, Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as though exhausted.

“So you've said all that in your testimony?” Ivan said, somewhat taken aback. He had meant to frighten him with the threat of repeating their conversation, and it turned out Smerdyakov had already reported all of it himself.
“What have I to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole truth,” Smerdyakov pronounced firmly.
“And have you told them every word of our conversation at the gate?”
“No, not every word.”
“And did you tell them that you can sham fits, as you boasted then?”
“No, I didn't tell them that either.”
“Tell me now, why did you send me to Tchermashnya that time?”
“I was afraid you'd go off to Moscow; Tchermashnya is nearer, anyway.”
“You're lying; you suggested going away yourself; you told me to get out of the way of trouble.”

“That was simply out of affection and my sincere devotion to you, foreseeing trouble in the house, wanting to spare you. Only I wanted to spare myself even more. That's why I told you to get out of harm's way, so you might understand that there would be trouble in the house, and would stay at home to protect your father.”
“You might have said it more directly, you blockhead!” Ivan suddenly fired up.

“How could I have said it more directly back then? It was just my fear that made me speak, and you might have gotten angry, too. Of course, I might well have worried that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and carry away that money, because he considered it as good as his own; but who could have told that it would end in a murder like this? I thought he'd only carry off the three thousand that lay under the master's mattress in the envelope — and you see, he's murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”
“But if you yourself say it couldn't be guessed, how was I supposed to have guessed it and stayed home? You're contradicting yourself!” Ivan said, pondering.
“You might have guessed from my sending you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow.”
“How could I have guessed it from that?”
Smerdyakov seemed much exhausted, and again he was silent for a minute.

“You might have guessed from the fact of my asking you not to go to Moscow but to Tchermashnya, that I wanted you nearer, because Moscow's a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you weren't far away, wouldn't be so bold. And if anything had happened, you could have come to protect me too, because I warned you of Grigory Vassilyevitch's illness, and that I was afraid of having a fit. And when I explained those knocks to you, by which someone could get in to the deceased, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you'd guess yourself he was bound to do something, and so wouldn't go to Tchermashnya at all, but would stay.”
“He talks very coherently,” Ivan thought, “though he does mumble; what's the derangement of his faculties that Herzenstube talked of?”
“You're being cunning with me, damn you!” he exclaimed, getting angry.
“But I thought at the time that you quite guessed,” Smerdyakov parried with the simplest air.
“If I'd guessed, I would have stayed,” Ivan cried.
“Why, I thought it was because you'd guessed that you went away in such a hurry, only to get out of trouble, only to run away and save yourself in your fright.”
“You think everyone is as great a coward as yourself?”
“Forgive me, I thought you were like me.”

“Of course, I ought to have guessed,” Ivan said, agitated. “And I did guess there was some mischief brewing on your part ... only you're lying, you're lying again,” he cried, suddenly remembering. “Do you remember how you came up to the carriage and said to me, ‘It's always worth while speaking to a clever man'? So you were glad I was going away, since you praised me?”
Smerdyakov sighed again and again. A trace of color came into his face.

“If I was pleased,” he said rather breathlessly, “it was simply because you agreed not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya. Because it was nearer, at any rate. Only when I said those words to you, it was not by way of praise, but of reproach. You didn't understand it.”
“What reproach?”
“Why, that foreseeing such a calamity, you deserted your own father, and wouldn't protect us, because I might have been taken up at any time for stealing that three thousand.”
“Damn you!” Ivan swore again. “Wait — did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?”
“I told them everything just as it was.”
Ivan wondered to himself again.

“If I thought of anything back then,” he began again, “it was solely of some wickedness on your part. Dmitri might kill him, but that he would steal — I didn't believe that back then. But I was prepared for any wickedness from you. You told me yourself you could sham a fit. What did you say that for?”

“It was just out of my simplicity — and I've never shammed a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it then to show off to you. It was just foolishness. I liked you so much at the time, and was open-hearted with you.”
“My brother directly accuses you of the murder and the theft.”

“What else is there left for him to do?” Smerdyakov said, with a bitter grin. “And who'll believe him with all the proofs against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say after that? But never mind him! He's trembling to save himself.”
He slowly stopped speaking; then suddenly, as if on reflection, added:

“And look here again. He wants to throw it on me and make out it's the work of my hands — I've heard that already. But as to my being clever at shamming a fit: would I have told you beforehand I could sham one, if I really had had such a design on your father? If I'd been planning such a murder, could I have been such a fool as to give such evidence against myself in advance? And to his son, too! Upon my word! Is that likely? As if such a thing could be — it's never happened. No one hears this talk of ours now except Providence itself, and if you were to tell of it to the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch, you might defend me completely by doing so, because who would be likely to be such a criminal if he's so open-hearted in advance? Anyone can see that.”

“Well —” and Ivan got up to cut the conversation short, struck by Smerdyakov's last argument. “I don't suspect you at all, and I think it's absurd, in fact, to suspect you. On the contrary, I'm grateful to you for setting my mind at rest. Now I'm going, but I'll come again. Meanwhile, good-bye. Get well. Is there anything you want?”
“I'm very grateful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn't forget me, and provides me with whatever I need, out of her kindness. Good people visit me every day.”
“Good-bye. But I won't mention your being able to sham a fit, and I don't advise you to either,” something made Ivan say suddenly.
“I quite understand. And if you don't speak of that, I'll say nothing of that conversation of ours at the gate.”

Then it happened that Ivan went out, and only after going a dozen steps along the corridor did he suddenly feel that there was an insulting significance in Smerdyakov's last words. He was almost on the point of turning back, but it was only a passing impulse, and muttering, “Nonsense!” he walked out of the hospital.

His chief feeling was one of relief at the fact that it was Mitya, not Smerdyakov, who had committed the murder, though you might have expected him to feel the opposite. He didn't want to analyze the reason for this feeling, and even felt a positive revulsion at prying into his own sensations. He felt as though he wanted to hurry up and forget something. In the following days he became convinced of Mitya's guilt as he learned the full weight of evidence against him. There was evidence from people of no importance — Fenya and her mother, for instance — but the effect of it was almost overpowering. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern, and at Plotnikov's shop, as well as the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence seemed conclusive. It was the details that were so damning. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers almost as much as Grigory's evidence about the open door. Grigory's wife, Marfa, in answer to Ivan's questions, declared that Smerdyakov had been lying all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed,” and that although she was a sound sleeper, she had woken several times and heard him moaning. “He was moaning the whole time, moaning continually.”
Talking to Herzenstube and giving it as his opinion that Smerdyakov was not mad, only rather weak, Ivan only drew from the old man a subtle smile.

“Do you know how he spends his time now?” he asked. “Learning lists of French words by heart. He has an exercise book under his pillow with the French words written out in Russian letters for him by someone — he he he!”

Ivan ended by dismissing all doubts. He couldn't think of Dmitri without repulsion. Only one thing was strange, however. Alyosha kept insisting that Dmitri was not the murderer, and that “in all probability” Smerdyakov was. Ivan always felt that Alyosha's opinion meant a great deal to him, and so he was astonished at it now. Another strange thing was that Alyosha made no attempt to talk about Mitya with Ivan — he never brought up the subject and only answered his questions. This, too, struck Ivan particularly.

But he was very much preoccupied at that time with something quite apart from all that. On his return from Moscow, he had abandoned himself hopelessly to his mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin to speak of this new passion of Ivan's, which left its mark on all the rest of his life: that would make the subject of another novel, which I may perhaps never write. But I cannot omit to mention here that when Ivan, on leaving Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha, as I have already related, told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie: he loved her madly, though at times he hated her so that he could have murdered her. Many causes helped to bring about this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, she rushed on Ivan's return to meet him as her one salvation. She was hurt, insulted, humiliated in her feelings. And here the man had come back to her who had loved her so ardently before (oh, she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she considered so superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl didn't abandon herself altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. She was constantly tormented at the same time by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were many) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had called to Alyosha “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything. But of all this, later.

He did, in fact, for a time almost forget Smerdyakov's existence, and yet, a fortnight after his first visit to him, he began to be haunted by the same strange thoughts as before. It's enough to say that he was constantly asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, he had crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened to hear what his father was doing downstairs. Why had he recalled that afterwards with revulsion? Why, the next morning, had he been suddenly so depressed on the journey? Why, as he reached Moscow, had he said to himself, “I am a scoundrel”? And now he almost felt that these tormenting thoughts would even make him forget Katerina Ivanovna, so completely did they take hold of him again. It was just after feeling this that he met Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once, and put a question to him:

“Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterwards I told you in the yard that I reserved ‘the right to desire'? Tell me — did you think then that I desired father's death or not?”
“I did think so,” Alyosha answered softly.

“It was so, too; it was not a matter of guessing. But didn't you also fancy then that what I wished was just that ‘one reptile should devour another'; that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and as soon as possible ... and that I myself was even prepared to help bring that about?”
Alyosha turned rather pale, and looked silently into his brother's face.
“Speak!” Ivan cried. “I want above all to know what you thought then. I want the truth, the truth!”
He drew a deep breath, looking angrily at Alyosha before the answer came.
“Forgive me, I did think that too, at the time,” Alyosha whispered, and he didn't add one softening phrase.

“Thanks,” Ivan snapped, and, leaving Alyosha, he walked quickly on his way. From that time Alyosha noticed that Ivan began obviously avoiding him and seemed even to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha gave up going to see him. Immediately after that meeting with him, Ivan didn't go home but went straight to Smerdyakov again.
